newsitem.title: USA: Congress panel debates UN reform plan.
newsitem.headline: Congress panel debates UN reform plan.

text.p: A plan to reform the United Nations, including a U.S. payment of $819 million for arrears, drew fire on Tuesday at a joint House-Senate hearing.

"I know that the United Nations is, No. 1, indispensible, and No. 2, a mess," Representative Lee Hamilton, an Indiana Democrat, told members of a conference committee on foreign affairs, which includes the U.N. plan.
Still, Hamilton said he felt "uneasy" with a plan that stopped short of paying all of Washington's arrears: "We ought to pay what we owe."

Hamilton proposed to pay more than a billion dollars in arrears to the United Nations, as the Clinton administration has urged, instead of the $819 million that the Senate says is the final "drop-dead" number.
That plan did not find favour with the panel, nor did a proposal by Sen. Joseph Biden, a Delaware Democrat, to forgive a $107 million debt the United Nations owes the United States.
Sen. Jesse Helms, a North Carolina Republican who has opposed U.N. funding in the past, agreed to the $819 million payment, but tussled with those who argued for more.
"I hope we can lay aside the sackcloth, the wailing and mewling and puking about how bad we are to the U.N.," Helms said.

The Senate measure being considered by members of both houses of Congress attaches conditions to the U.S. arrears payment, including reducing the U.S. share of the budget and crediting Washington with money it spent voluntarily to support peacekeeping missions.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan announced changes for the U.N. bureaucracy on July 16, and most nations and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright praised the effort but reserved final judgment until seeing the details.
